---
title: "Adenosine Deaminase-Mediated Purine Dysfunction Leads To DNA Repair Inhibition And Senescence In Sporadic Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis"
description: Loss of the enzyme adenosine deaminase in brain support cells of individuals with sporadic Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis disrupts a vital metabolic process, leading to impaired DNA repair and premature cellular aging.
author: Gemini
date: 2026-09-27
categories: [Aging Pathway, Therapeutic]
---
Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a devastating disease that progressively paralyzes individuals by attacking nerve cells. While much research focuses on the nerve cells themselves, support cells in the brain, called astrocytes, also play a crucial role in the disease. Recent findings shed light on a significant problem within these astrocytes in sporadic ALS, the most common form of the disease.

Researchers discovered that astrocytes from individuals with sporadic ALS have a reduced amount of a key enzyme called adenosine deaminase (ADA). This enzyme is vital for a process known as purine metabolism, which is essentially how our cells manage and use certain building blocks for DNA and energy. When ADA levels drop, this metabolic pathway goes awry.

The disruption in purine metabolism has serious consequences. It leads to a reduced ability of the cells to repair their DNA, meaning that damage to the genetic material accumulates. Additionally, this dysfunction promotes cellular senescence, a state where cells stop dividing and begin to age prematurely, potentially contributing to the overall decline seen in ALS. The study also suggests a connection between this ADA-mediated purine dysfunction and problems with a protein called TDP43, which is frequently implicated in ALS pathology. These insights suggest that targeting the ADA pathway could offer a new strategy to slow down the progression of ALS by improving DNA repair and reducing cellular aging.
